Vignette: A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Sex: Male

Analysis: The patient presents with classic signs of acute limb ischemia (pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis) that began <6 hours ago. Subclinical specialization: Emergency

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 8 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Scald burns to anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and face after boiling water spill (~45 min ago)  

Analysis: The patient has sustained thermal injuries covering ~20 % TBSA. Superficial partial‑thickness (erythema with blisters) involves the chest and abdomen, while deep partial‑ to full‑thickness (waxy white, insensate) involves both forearms. No circumferential burns are present, and airway examination is normal (no singed nasal hairs, hoarseness, or stridor), making inhalation injury unlikely. Vital signs show tachycardia (HR 152) likely pain‑related; blood pressure is acceptable for age. The calculated Parkland formula (2 240 mL LR in 24 h) has been initiated, and analgesia with morphine has been given. Key considerations include adequate fluid resuscitation, pain control, tetanus prophylaxis, wound management, monitoring for compartment syndrome, and evaluation for burn‑center referral (deep burns >10 % TBSA in a child). Differential diagnoses such as associated trauma or infection are low priority given the current findings.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CBC, basic metabolic panel, coagulation profile, blood type & screen, urine output monitoring (catheter or Foley), wound cultures if infection suspected, chest X‑ray only if airway concerns develop  

Conclusion: An 8‑year‑old boy with 20 % TBSA scald burns (mixed superficial and deep partial/full thickness) requiring immediate fluid resuscitation, analgesia, wound care, and close monitoring; airway is intact, but deep forearm burns warrant specialist evaluation and possible burn‑center transfer.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations:  
1. **Fluid resuscitation** – Continue Parkland formula: deliver the first half of the calculated 2 240 mL LR within the first 8 h from burn (≈1 120 mL), then the remaining half over the next 16 h. Adjust rate to maintain urine output ≥ 1 mL/kg/h.  
2. **Analgesia** – Continue opioid analgesia (e.g., morphine) with adjuncts such as acetaminophen or ketamine infusion for multimodal pain control.  
3. **Tetanus prophylaxis** – Administer tetanus toxoid vaccine if immunization status is unknown or >5 years since last dose; give tetanus immune globulin if wound is heavily contaminated.  
4. **Wound care** – Gently cleanse burns with sterile saline. Apply a topical antimicrobial dressing (e.g., silver sulfadiazine or mafenide acetate) to superficial partial‑thickness areas. For deep partial/full‑thickness forearm burns, consider early excision and grafting; keep the area moist and protected.  
5. **Monitoring** –  
   - Hourly vital signs and pain assessment.  
   - Hourly urine output (target ≥ 1 mL/kg/h).  
   - Serial neurovascular checks of the forearms (capillary refill, sensation, motor function).  
   - Observe for signs of compartment syndrome (increasing pain, swelling, decreased pulses).  
6. **Laboratory evaluation** – Obtain CBC, BMP, coagulation panel, and blood type & screen on admission; repeat as clinically indicated.  
7. **Burn‑center referral** – Because the patient has deep partial/full‑thickness burns involving both forearms (>10 % TBSA in a child) and mixed‑depth burns, arrange transfer to a pediatric burn center for possible early excision/grafting and specialized care.  
8. **Psychological support** – Provide age‑appropriate reassurance, involve child life services, and consider parental presence to reduce distress.  
9. **Disposition** – Admit to a pediatric intensive care or burn unit for continued resuscitation, monitoring, and definitive burn management.  

Notes: None.

Vignette:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician reporting 8 months of near-constant excessive worry about multiple domains of her life including work performance, finances, health, and her children's safety. She describes an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it is disproportionate. She reports associated restlessness, muscle tension predominantly in her neck and shoulders, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. She has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit. She denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, or traumatic experiences. She has no prior psychiatric history and takes no medications. She drinks one cup of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral trapezius muscle tightness but is otherwise unremarkable. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. GAD-7 score is 16 indicating severe anxiety.

Age: 29  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Persistent, excessive worry across multiple life domains for 8 months with associated restlessness, neck/shoulder muscle tension, insomnia, irritability, and difficulty concentrating.  
Analysis: The patient’s presentation fulfills DSM‑5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD): >6 months of pervasive worry, perceived inability to control the worry, and ≥3 associated symptoms (restlessness, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, impaired concentration). Thyroid function is normal, caffeine intake is minimal, and there is no history of panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive‑compulsive symptoms, trauma, or substance misuse, making secondary medical causes less likely. Differential considerations include hyperthyroidism (ruled out), stimulant‑induced anxiety, other anxiety disorders, and depressive disorder; however, the symptom pattern and GAD‑7 score of 16 (severe) support primary GAD.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: 29‑year‑old woman meets criteria for severe Generalized Anxiety Disorder.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  
Recommendations:  
1. Initiate evidence‑based treatment:  
   - **Psychotherapy:** Refer for cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) focusing on worry exposure, cognitive restructuring, and relaxation training.  
   - **Pharmacotherapy:** Consider starting an SSRI (e.g., sertraline 25 mg daily, titrating as tolerated) or SNRI (e.g., venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg daily) after discussing benefits/risks. Obtain baseline labs (CBC, CMP) if prescribing medication.  
2. Lifestyle & self‑care:  
   - Limit caffeine to ≤1 cup/day (already low).  
   - Continue regular aerobic exercise; aim for ≥150 min/week.  
   - Implement sleep hygiene (consistent bedtime, screen‑free wind‑down).  
   - Practice progressive muscle relaxation or mindfulness meditation daily.  
3. Monitoring:  
   - Schedule follow‑up in 4–6 weeks to assess symptom response and medication tolerability.  
   - Screen for depressive symptoms (PHQ‑9) and suicidal ideation at each visit.  
   - If symptoms markedly worsen or suicidal thoughts emerge, arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation.  
Notes: None.

Age: 40  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Persistent year‑round nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea worsening with dust exposure.  
Analysis: The patient’s chronic, bilateral, pale‑boggy nasal mucosa, transverse nasal crease, and symptom pattern triggered by indoor dust strongly suggest perennial allergic rhinitis, most likely due to dust‑mite exposure. Absence of asthma, nasal polyps, or purulent discharge makes allergic rhinitis more likely than non‑allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, or structural obstruction.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin prick testing or serum specific IgE for indoor allergens (e.g., dust mite) – to confirm allergen sensitivity.  
Conclusion: Chronic perennial allergic rhinitis, probably dust‑mite mediated.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  
Recommendations:  
1. Initiate intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone) daily.  
2. Continue or add a second‑generation oral antihistamine for breakthrough symptoms.  
3. Implement allergen‑avoidance measures:  
   - Use allergen‑impermeable mattress and pillow encasements.  
   - Wash bedding weekly in hot water (>130 °F).  
   - Remove or replace wall‑to‑wall carpeting; use HEPA vacuum with a sealed bag.  
   - Maintain indoor humidity <50 % to limit dust‑mite proliferation.  
4. Perform saline nasal irrigation twice daily to improve mucosal clearance.  
5. Arrange allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE) to confirm specific sensitivities; consider referral to allergy/immunology if testing positive.  
6. Re‑evaluate in 4–6 weeks; if symptoms remain uncontrolled, consider adding a leukotriene receptor antagonist or a short course of oral corticosteroids.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. case_text:
Vignette:
A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 16  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, fatigue, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis with soft‑palate petechiae, and a faint macular rash.  

Analysis: The combination of prolonged fever, exudative pharyngitis, cervical lymph node enlargement, soft‑palate petechiae, and a diffuse macular rash in an adolescent strongly suggests infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein‑Barr virus. The rash could be a viral exanthem or, if antibiotics were inadvertently given, a drug‑induced rash, but no antibiotic exposure is reported. Differential diagnoses include streptococcal pharyngitis (which can also cause exudates and fever) and other viral pharyngitides (e.g., adenovirus). The presence of palatal petechiae and the rash tip the balance toward EBV infection, but a rapid strep test is useful to exclude concurrent group A Streptococcus, which would alter management.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for Group A Streptococcus (throat swab)  
- Complete blood count with differential (to look for lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes)  
- Heterophile antibody test (Monospot) or EBV‑specific serology  

Conclusion: The clinical picture is most consistent with infectious mononucleosis (EBV) with a need to rule out streptococcal co‑infection.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations:  
1. Obtain throat swab for rapid strep test and send for culture if positive.  
2. Order CBC with differential and heterophile antibody test (Monospot); if negative but suspicion remains, consider EBV IgM/IgG serology.  
3. Provide supportive care: adequate hydration, antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for fever and sore throat, and throat lozenges or warm saline gargles.  
4. Advise the patient to avoid contact sports or heavy lifting for at least 3–4 weeks, pending evaluation for splenomegaly (palpate abdomen; consider ultrasound if clinically indicated).  
5. Counsel to avoid prescribing or taking amoxicillin or other β‑lactam antibiotics unless a bacterial infection is confirmed, to prevent a rash.  
6. Arrange follow‑up in 5–7 days or sooner if symptoms worsen (e.g., difficulty breathing, severe neck swelling, or signs of airway compromise).  

Notes: None.

Vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. He has had no significant past medical history and immunizations are not up to date (parents declined some vaccines). On examination, the child is sitting upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with his neck extended and jaw thrust forward. He is drooling profusely and appears anxious and toxic-appearing. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 92% on room air. Inspiratory stridor is audible without a stethoscope. His voice is muffled and he refuses to speak or drink. A soft tissue lateral neck X-ray obtained reveals a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling. Anesthesiology and ENT are urgently called for airway management.

Analysis: The child presents with classic signs of acute epiglottitis—high fever, drooling, tripod positioning, muffled (“hot‑potato”) voice, and a thumb‑sign on lateral neck X‑ray indicating epiglottic swelling. These findings, together with the rapid progression over 6 hours and toxic appearance, point to a bacterial epiglottitis (most commonly Haemophilus influenzae type b) with imminent airway obstruction. Key differentials include viral croup, bacterial tracheitis, and peritonsillar abscess, but the thumb sign and severe drooling make epiglottitis the leading diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (airway assessment and management take precedence; diagnosis already confirmed by imaging).  
Conclusion: Acute epiglottitis with impending airway compromise in a 4‑year‑old boy.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

1. **Airway management** – Keep the child upright, calm, and in a tripod position.

   - Have video laryngoscope, rigid bronchoscope, and surgical airway set‑up (cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy) ready.  
   - Avoid any attempts at oral examination that could provoke airway collapse.  
2. **Oxygenation** – Administer humidified 100 % oxygen via face mask; monitor SpO₂ continuously.  
3. **IV access** – Establish large‑bore IV lines; obtain blood for CBC, CRP, blood cultures.

5. **Adjunctive therapy** – Consider a single dose of IV dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg) to reduce edema.  
6. **Monitoring** – Continuous cardiac, pulse‑ox, and respiratory monitoring; transfer to pediatric ICU post‑intubation.  
7. **Vaccination review** – Counsel parents on the importance of completing the Hib vaccine series after stabilization.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Progressive periumbilical discomfort now localized to the right lower quadrant with decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one loose stool.  
Analysis: The patient’s history of gradually worsening RLQ pain, mild leukocytosis (WBC 11,200/mcL), and CT findings of a dilated (14 mm) appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection are classic for acute appendicitis with early perforation. The lack of fever or peritoneal signs suggests a contained perforation rather than generalized peritonitis. Main differentials such as right‑sided diverticulitis, cecal neoplasm, or epiploic appendagitis are less likely given the imaging confirmation of an inflamed appendix.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute appendicitis with early (contained) perforation.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  
Recommendations:  
- Obtain immediate surgical consultation for urgent appendectomy (laparoscopic preferred if feasible).  
- Initiate broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin‑tazobactam).  
- Keep patient NPO, start IV fluids, and provide analgesia as needed.  
- Optimize comorbid conditions pre‑operatively: ensure adequate glucose control for diabetes and assess cardiac status given known CAD (consider peri‑operative cardiac clearance if indicated).  
- Order baseline pre‑operative labs (CBC, CMP, coagulation profile) if not already obtained.  
- Post‑operative monitoring for signs of sepsis or intra‑abdominal infection.  
Notes: None

Age: 29  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and mild headache that worsen with prolonged computer use.  
Analysis: The patient’s symptoms are classic for digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome). Supporting facts include prolonged screen time (10–12 h/day), improvement on weekends, normal visual acuity (20/20), intact extraocular movements, reactive pupils, only mild conjunctival injection, and otherwise normal anterior segment and fundus. Differential considerations such as uncorrected refractive error, significant dry‑eye disease, ocular surface pathology, migraine, or intracranial process are less likely given the normal exam and lack of red‑flag symptoms (no blurred vision, photopsia, eye pain, or neurologic deficits).  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The presentation is consistent with computer‑related visual fatigue (digital eye strain) without evidence of ocular pathology requiring further work‑up.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  
Recommendations:  
- Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something ≥20 feet away for at least 20 seconds.  
- Take scheduled breaks (5‑10 minutes) every hour to rest the eyes and stretch.  
- Optimize ergonomics: monitor top at or slightly below eye level, ~20‑30 inches away, reduce glare, use matte screen filter if needed.  
- Adjust screen settings: increase text size, reduce brightness/contrast, use “night mode” or blue‑light filter in the evening.  
- Use preservative‑free artificial tears 2‑4 times daily to relieve dryness.  
- Maintain adequate ambient humidity; consider a humidifier if environment is dry.  
- Ensure proper hydration and regular blinking, especially when concentrating.  
- Consider over‑the‑counter computer glasses with slight near‑vision addition if symptoms persist despite behavioral measures.  
- Schedule a follow‑up eye examination in 4–6 weeks if symptoms do not improve or worsen, or if new visual changes develop.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 56  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Shortness of breath and increased productive cough of several days, preceded by rhinorrhea.  
Analysis: The patient is a long‑term heavy smoker with a chronic productive morning cough, consistent with chronic bronchitis (a phenotype of COPD). The acute worsening over 3 days with rhinorrhea suggests a viral upper‑respiratory infection triggering an acute COPD exacerbation. Absence of fever, chills, hemoptysis, weight loss, or severe dyspnea makes pneumonia, lung cancer, or heart failure less likely, but they must be excluded with appropriate testing.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Pulse oximetry (baseline oxygen saturation)  
- Chest radiograph (to rule out pneumonia or other infiltrates)  
- Spirometry (post‑bronchodilator) to confirm and stage COPD  
- Complete blood count (to assess for infection)  
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD) likely secondary to a viral upper‑respiratory infection, without immediate red‑flag features.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations:  
1. Obtain pulse oximetry and chest X‑ray today; if saturation < 92 % or X‑ray shows infiltrate, consider urgent evaluation.  
2. Schedule spirometry within the next 2 weeks to confirm COPD severity and guide long‑term therapy.  
3. Initiate a short‑acting bronchodilator (e.g., albuterol inhaler) as needed for dyspnea.  
4. Counsel on smoking cessation; offer nicotine replacement, counseling, and pharmacotherapy (e.g., varenicline).  
5. Recommend influenza and pneumococcal vaccination if not already received.  
6. Use a trial of a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days) if symptoms worsen or oxygen saturation declines.  
7. Antibiotics are not indicated at this time given lack of purulent sputum, fever, or leukocytosis; reassess if bacterial signs develop.  
8. Follow up in 1–2 weeks to assess response; earlier return if worsening dyspnea, fever, chest pain, or new hemoptysis.  
Notes: None.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 5 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy erythematous papules on forearms and lower legs after outdoor play.  
Analysis: The child presents with multiple small (3‑5 mm) erythematous papules with central puncta, limited to exposed areas (forearms, lower legs) and onset within 24 h of outdoor exposure. The lesions are pruritic, without swelling, cellulitis, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy, fever, or systemic symptoms. This pattern is classic for papular urticaria or insect‑bite hypersensitivity, common in young children after exposure to arthropod bites. Differential considerations include:  
- Insect bite reaction (most likely)  
- Mild allergic contact dermatitis (possible but lesions are papular with puncta)  
- Viral exanthem (less likely: would be more diffuse, may have systemic signs)  
- Early impetigo (no crusting or purulent signs)  
Given the benign appearance, lack of systemic involvement, and typical distribution, no urgent investigations are required.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with a benign insect‑bite reaction/papular urticaria.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  
Recommendations:  
1. Symptomatic relief – give an age‑appropriate oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 5 mg once daily) to reduce itching.  
2. Topical therapy – apply a low‑potency corticosteroid cream (e.g., 1% hydrocortisone) to affected areas twice daily for 3‑5 days.  
3. Non‑pharmacologic measures – cool compresses and keep nails trimmed to minimize excoriation.  
4. Education – advise mother to monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection (increased redness, warmth, pus, pain) and to seek care if these develop.  
5. Prevention – consider using insect repellent and protective clothing during outdoor activities.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 24  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Dysuria and urinary frequency progressing over 3 days to right flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea and one episode of vomiting.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic signs of an upper urinary tract infection (fever > 102 °F, flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness, rigors, nausea/vomiting) and urinalysis confirming a bacterial infection (leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, bacteriuria). Vital signs show tachycardia and borderline low blood pressure, suggesting systemic involvement and possible early sepsis. The most likely diagnosis is acute pyelonephritis. Differential considerations include complicated pyelonephritis (e.g., obstruction, renal abscess), perinephric abscess, and less likely renal colic or pelvic inflammatory disease (no vaginal discharge, negative pregnancy test).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Complete blood count with differential  
- Basic metabolic panel (electrolytes, renal function)  
- Blood cultures (two sets)  
- Urine culture and sensitivity (if not already obtained)  
- Renal ultrasound (to assess for obstruction or abscess if clinical course does not improve)  

Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis in a young, non‑pregnant woman with systemic signs, requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy and monitoring for possible complications.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Urology  

Recommendations:  
1. Admit to hospital for intravenous antimicrobial therapy (e.g., ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24 h or a fluoroquinolone pending sensitivities).  
2. Obtain blood cultures and urine culture before starting antibiotics.  
3. Initiate aggressive IV hydration; provide anti‑emetics and analgesia as needed.  
4. Monitor vital signs, urine output, and laboratory trends (CBC, BMP) every 4–6 hours.  
5. If no clinical improvement within 48–72 hours, obtain renal ultrasound to evaluate for obstruction or abscess; consider CT abdomen/pelvis if indicated.  
6. Educate patient on completing the full course of antibiotics, signs of worsening infection, and importance of follow‑up with primary care or urology after discharge.  

Notes: None

Vignette:
A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. Sex: Male  
Complaint: Burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest for 5 days, followed by erythema, maculopapular rash, headache, malaise, and progression to clustered clear vesicles that later pustulated, ulcerated, and crusted.  
Analysis: The presentation is classic for herpes zoster (shingles) – prodromal unilateral thoracic pain, followed by a dermatomal erythematous rash that evolves to grouped vesicles and later crusts. The age (>50 years) and immunosenescence increase risk. Headache and malaise are common systemic symptoms. Main differentials (herpes simplex infection, contact dermatitis, cellulitis, allergic reaction) are less likely because of the dermatomal distribution, preceding neuropathic pain, and vesicular evolution. No signs of disseminated infection, ocular involvement, or immunocompromise are reported.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Classic unilateral thoracic herpes zoster in an elderly patient.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations:  
1. Initiate oral antiviral therapy (e.g., valacyclovir 1 g three times daily or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily) as soon as possible, ideally within 72 h of rash onset.  
2. Provide analgesia – acetaminophen or NSAIDs for mild pain; consider gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain; topical lidocaine patches may be added.  
3. Advise the patient to keep the lesions clean and covered to prevent secondary bacterial infection; consider topical antibiotic if signs of bacterial superinfection appear.  
4. Counsel regarding the risk of post‑herpetic neuralgia; schedule follow‑up in 1–2 weeks to assess pain control and healing.  
5. Review vaccination history – if the patient has not received the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix), discuss future vaccination after acute episode resolves.  
6. Educate the patient to seek urgent care if lesions become widespread, involve the eye, or if systemic symptoms worsen (fever, confusion).

baseline_protocol:
Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Continuous generalized tonic‑clonic seizure (status epilepticus) refractory to benzodiazepines  
Analysis: The patient is in convulsive status epilepticus. Evidence: >5 min of uninterrupted generalized tonic‑clonic activity, failure of intramuscular midazolam (10 mg) and intravenous lorazepam (4 mg) to achieve sustained seizure control. Vital signs show hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension, hypoxia, and cyanosis, indicating impending respiratory failure and autonomic instability. The most likely precipitant is missed levetiracetam doses, but other contributors (infection, metabolic derangement, drug levels, structural brain lesion) must be considered. Immediate priorities are airway protection, cessation of seizures with second‑line antiepileptic therapy, and identification of reversible causes.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Rapid‑sequence intubation kit (laryngoscope, endotracheal tube, sedatives, paralytics)  
- Bag‑valve‑mask and oxygen delivery devices  
- Cardiac monitor, continuous pulse oximetry, capnography  
- Point‑of‑care arterial blood gas (ABG)  
- Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, glucose (already checked), renal function, liver function, CBC, toxicology screen, levetiracetam level (if available)  
- Non‑contrast head CT (after airway/ventilation secured)  
- Continuous EEG (once stabilized)  
Conclusion: 28‑year‑old woman in refractory convulsive status epilepticus requiring emergent airway management and second‑line antiepileptic therapy, with work‑up for underlying precipitants.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations:  
1. **Airway & Breathing:** Perform rapid‑sequence intubation (e.g., etomidate + succinylcholine or ketamine + rocuronium) and initiate mechanical ventilation with 100 % O₂; confirm tube placement with capnography.  
2. **Seizure Control:**  
   - Continue a benzodiazepine infusion (e.g., midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/hr) if not already started.  
   - Administer a second‑line antiepileptic agent:  
     • Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV infusion (max 150 mg PE over 15 min) **or**  
     • Valproic acid 30 mg/kg IV infusion (max 3 g) **or**  
     • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g) if not contraindicated.  
3. **Hemodynamic & Temperature Management:** Treat hypertension with short‑acting IV agents (e.g., labetalol) if needed; initiate active cooling for temperature >38.5 °C.  
4. **Laboratory & Imaging Work‑up:** Obtain ABG, electrolytes, CBC, CMP, toxicology, and levetiracetam level; after airway secured, obtain emergent non‑contrast head CT to rule out acute intracranial pathology.  
5. **Monitoring:** Transfer to ICU; continuous EEG to assess for non‑convulsive status; maintain strict vitals, glucose, and oxygenation monitoring.  
6. **Address Underlying Cause:** Review medication adherence, insurance barriers, and arrange social work follow‑up; consider adjusting chronic antiepileptic regimen after stabilization.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.

criterion:

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 31  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral milky nipple discharge with breast tenderness, secondary amenorrhea (6 months), daily frontal/headaches, infertility, decreased libido, and vaginal dryness.  
Analysis: The patient has marked hyperprolactinemia (prolactin 500 µg/L) associated with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. MRI demonstrates a sellar mass (1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm) without optic chiasm compression. Normal TSH excludes hypothyroidism as a cause of elevated prolactin. No dopamine‑antagonist medications or chest wall pathology are reported. The constellation of findings is most consistent with a prolactin‑secreting pituitary macroadenoma (macroprolactinoma). Differential considerations (e.g., stalk effect from non‑functioning adenoma, other pituitary hormone deficiencies) are less likely given the markedly elevated prolactin and clinical picture. Absence of visual field deficits makes the situation non‑emergent but warrants prompt endocrine management.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Automated visual field testing (perimetry)  
- Full pituitary hormone panel: LH, FSH, estradiol, cortisol (AM), ACTH, IGF‑1, and repeat prolactin for baseline  
- Follow‑up MRI of the sellar region in 6–12 months (or sooner if symptoms evolve)  
Conclusion: Macroprolactinoma causing hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea, menstrual suppression, infertility, and headaches.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  
Recommendations:  
1. Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy (first‑line cabergoline 0.5 mg orally once weekly, titrate based on prolactin response and tolerance; bromocriptine as alternative).  
2. Re‑check serum prolactin in 4–6 weeks; adjust dose to achieve normal levels and restore ovulation.  
3. Obtain baseline automated visual field testing to document any subtle deficits and for future comparison.  
4. Order comprehensive pituitary hormone panel to assess for co‑existing deficiencies; replace any deficient hormones as indicated.  
5. Schedule repeat pituitary MRI in ~6 months to assess tumor size response.  
6. Counsel patient on fertility expectations: prolactin normalization often restores menstrual cycles and ovulation; refer to reproductive endocrinology if conception does not occur after 3–6 months of normalized prolactin.  
7. Address headache management: monitor response to dopamine agonist (often improves headaches); consider NSAID use as needed, but avoid excessive dosing.  
8. Provide support for mild depressive symptoms; consider referral to mental health services if symptoms persist.  
9. Advise patient to report any new visual changes, sudden worsening headaches, or neurological symptoms promptly.  
Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 44-year-old woman with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement presents with 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral medications down for 2 days. On examination, she is lethargic and appears critically ill with notable hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 72/38 (unresponsive to 2L IV normal saline), SpO2 95%. Skin turgor is markedly decreased. Labs: sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, glucose 52 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, random cortisol 1.2 mcg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval. IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg is administered immediately.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 44  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain with inability to retain oral medications, lethargy, severe hypotension refractory to fluids.  
Analysis: The patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents with vomiting/diarrhea leading to loss of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, profound volume depletion, hyponatremia (118 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (6.4 mEq/L), hypoglycemia (52 mg/dL), acute kidney injury (BUN 48, Cr 2.1 mg/dL), and refractory hypotension (72/38 mmHg). ECG shows peaked T waves, indicating hyperkalemia‑related cardiac risk. Random cortisol is low (1.2 µg/dL). These findings strongly support an adrenal crisis precipitated by gastroenteritis. Differential considerations (septic shock, acute gastroenteritis with dehydration, cardiac arrhythmia) are less likely given the known Addison disease, low cortisol, and classic electrolyte pattern.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring; repeat basic metabolic panel (electrolytes, renal function) every 2–4 h; serum cortisol and ACTH levels after hydrocortisone bolus; serum lactate; blood cultures; point‑of‑care glucose checks.  
Conclusion: Acute adrenal crisis secondary to abrupt loss of glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement in a patient with Addison disease, complicated by severe hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, hypoglycemia, and acute kidney injury.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  
Recommendations:  
1. **Glucocorticoid replacement** – Continue IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus (already given) followed by 200 mg/24 h either as continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 h.  
2. **Fluid resuscitation** – Rapid isotonic saline (1 L bolus) with 5% dextrose as needed to correct hypoglycemia; titrate to achieve MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.  
3. **Electrolyte management** –  
   - Hyperkalemia: Give IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% over 5 min (cardioprotection), followed by regular insulin 10 U with 25 g dextrose, and consider nebulized albuterol. Re‑check K⁺ q1‑2 h.  
   - Hyponatremia: Correct gradually with saline; avoid rapid overcorrection.  
4. **Glucose** – Administer 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV push if glucose <70 mg/dL; then start D5W infusion as needed.  
5. **Monitoring** – Continuous cardiac telemetry, frequent vitals, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h, repeat labs (BMP, glucose, lactate) q2‑4 h.  
6. **Mineralocorticoid replacement** – Once hemodynamically stable and on glucocorticoid infusion, add fludrocortisone 0.1 mg PO daily (or IV if unable to take PO).  
7. **Infection work‑up** – Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; consider empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics if sepsis suspected after cultures.  
8. **Transition to oral therapy** – When stable (BP > 90/60 mmHg, tolerating PO, electrolytes normalized), taper IV hydrocortisone to oral hydrocortisone 20 mg AM, 10 mg early afternoon, 10 mg late afternoon, and resume fludrocortisone.  
9. **Patient education** – Reinforce sick‑day rules: double‑dose oral hydrocortisone for mild illness, seek emergency care for vomiting/diarrhea, wear medical alert ID.  
Notes: None.

Vignette: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of the right lower leg with systemic toxicity.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of necrotizing fasciitis: severe pain disproportionate to exam, tense dusky erythema, purplish discoloration, hemorrhagic bullae, palpable crepitus, rapid expansion of erythema despite oral antibiotics, systemic signs of sepsis (fever 39.8 °C, tachycardia 128 bpm, hypotension 92/56 mmHg, lactate 4.6 mmol/L), markedly elevated WBC (28,200/µL), high CRP, hyponatremia, acute kidney injury, and a LRINEC score of 10. CT imaging confirms gas tracking along fascial planes. Differential diagnoses such as uncomplicated cellulitis, deep‑vein thrombosis, or gas gangrene are less likely given the combination of severe pain out of proportion, rapid progression, and imaging findings; necrotizing fasciitis remains the most probable and life‑threatening diagnosis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (immediate surgical exploration is indicated; further imaging would delay care).  

Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg with septic shock requiring emergent surgical debridement and broad‑spectrum antimicrobial therapy.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  

Recommendations:  
1. **Activate massive transfusion/critical care protocol** – begin aggressive IV crystalloid resuscitation (e.g., 30 mL/kg bolus) and initiate vasopressors (norepinephrine) for persistent hypotension.  
2. **Empiric broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics** immediately (e.g., vancomycin + piperacillin‑tazobactam; consider adding clindamycin for toxin suppression).  
3. **Urgent surgical consultation** – transport to the operating room for immediate fasciotomy and extensive debridement; do not delay for further imaging.  
4. **Blood cultures** (≥2 sets) and wound cultures **before** antibiotics if it will not delay therapy.  
5. **Intensive care unit admission** post‑operatively for hemodynamic monitoring, renal support, and glucose control (target 140‑180 mg/dL).  
6. **Adjuncts** – tetanus prophylaxis if immunization status unknown; consider hyperbaric oxygen therapy if available and not delaying surgery.  
7. **Serial labs** – repeat CBC, CMP, lactate, coagulation profile, and CRP every 4–6 h to gauge response.

Vignette:
A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 14 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken  
Analysis: The patient presents with an acute onset (<24 h) of watery, non‑bloody diarrhea (≈6 stools/day), mild abdominal cramping, low‑grade fever, and mild tachycardia, all occurring after a known exposure to potentially contaminated poultry. The clinical picture is most consistent with an acute infectious gastroenteritis, likely bacterial (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella) given the undercooked chicken exposure. He is hemodynamically stable, able to tolerate oral fluids, and has no red‑flag features such as high‑grade fever, blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, or signs of significant dehydration. Differential considerations include viral gastroenteritis, food‑borne toxin ingestion, and early inflammatory bowel disease, but the exposure history and presentation favor an acute bacterial infection.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (consider stool culture or PCR if symptoms persist >48‑72 h or if red‑flag signs develop)  

Conclusion: Mild to moderate acute bacterial gastroenteritis with mild dehydration; patient is stable and can be managed with oral rehydration and supportive care.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations:  
1. Continue oral rehydration therapy (ORS) – aim for 50‑100 mL/kg of fluid over the next 4‑6 h, adjusting for ongoing losses.  
2. Encourage a bland diet (e.g., bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) as tolerated.  
3. Use anti‑emetics (e.g., ondansetron) if vomiting limits oral intake.  
4. Avoid antidiarrheal agents (e.g., loperamide) in this pediatric patient.  
5. Monitor for worsening dehydration (increased tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output) or red‑flag symptoms (high fever >101.5 °F, blood/mucus in stool, severe abdominal pain).  
6. Return to care or seek urgent evaluation if any red‑flag signs develop.  
7. If diarrhea persists beyond 48‑72 h, or if the patient develops fever >102 °F, blood in stool, or severe symptoms, obtain stool studies (culture/PCR) and consider empiric antibiotic therapy per local guidelines.  

Notes: None.

2. Initiate empiric proton‑pump inhibitor therapy (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg daily) while awaiting diagnostic work‑up.  
3. Arrange for H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen). If positive, treat with standard triple/quadruple therapy.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

Age: 34
Sex: Male
Complaint: Inversion injury to left ankle with inability to bear weight, swelling, and pain over lateral malleolus.
Analysis: The patient sustained an inversion mechanism with audible crack, leading to a non‑displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) on radiographs. Significant lateral swelling and point tenderness over the distal fibula, with an intact neurovascular exam and no medial tenderness, support an isolated lateral malleolar fracture. The lack of talar shift and a non‑displaced fracture suggest a stable injury without syndesmotic disruption. Main differentials (e.g., high‑ankle sprain, deltoid ligament injury, displaced fracture) are less likely given imaging and exam findings.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Stable, non‑displaced Weber B distal fibular fracture of the left ankle with intact neurovascular status.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: 
- Apply RICE measures (rest, ice, compression, elevation).  
- Immobilize the ankle in a short‑leg cast or functional walking boot.  
- Advise non‑weight‑bearing for approximately 2 weeks; transition to protected weight‑bearing as tolerated thereafter.  
- Prescribe analgesics (e.g., NSAIDs) as needed, avoiding excessive dosing.  
- Schedule orthopedic follow‑up within 7 days for clinical reassessment and repeat radiographs at 2 weeks to confirm maintained alignment.  
- Initiate physiotherapy after immobilization to restore range of motion, strength, and proprioception.  
- Educate the patient on signs of complications (increasing pain, swelling, numbness, discoloration) and to return promptly if they occur.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man presents with difficulty falling and staying asleep over the past 5 nights. He recently took on a major project at work with a tight deadline and reports feeling anxious about it. He estimates sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night and experiencing daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, or suicidal ideation. He has no history of sleep disorders. He consumes coffee until mid-afternoon. On examination, he is well-groomed but appears mildly fatigued. Vital signs are normal. Neurological exam and mental status exam are unremarkable.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Difficulty falling and staying asleep for the past 5 nights, associated with work‑related anxiety, daytime fatigue, and difficulty concentrating.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute insomnia that began after taking on a high‑stress work project. Key supporting facts are: recent onset (5 nights), clear stressor, normal physical and mental status exam, absence of depressive symptoms or suicidal ideation, no prior sleep disorder, and ongoing caffeine use into the afternoon (a known sleep disruptor). The most likely diagnosis is stress‑related (adjustment) insomnia, possibly exacerbated by caffeine. Important differentials to keep in mind are primary insomnia, caffeine‑induced insomnia, mood disorders (e.g., depression), medical causes (e.g., hyperthyroidism, sleep apnea), and substance use. No red‑flag symptoms are present to suggest an urgent medical work‑up.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute insomnia secondary to work‑related stress and excessive caffeine intake.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  
Recommendations:  
1. **Sleep hygiene counseling** – keep a regular bedtime/wake‑time schedule, reserve the bedroom for sleep, limit screen exposure 1 hour before bed.  
2. **Caffeine reduction** – discontinue coffee after 12 pm; consider switching to decaffeinated beverages in the afternoon.  
3. **Stress‑management techniques** – brief relaxation exercises, deep‑breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation before bedtime.  
4. **Cognitive‑behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT‑I)** – refer for CBT‑I if insomnia persists beyond 2–3 weeks.  
5. **Pharmacologic bridge (if needed)** – short‑term use of a low‑dose, non‑benzodiazepine hypnotic (e.g., zolpidem 5 mg) may be considered for ≤2 weeks, with caution and patient education.  
6. **Follow‑up** – re‑evaluate in 2–4 weeks; if insomnia continues >4 weeks, worsens, or new mood symptoms appear, consider formal psychiatric assessment and possible screening labs (TSH, CBC) to rule out medical contributors.  
Notes: None

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.
